title: LPG tanker Gas Husky sinks off Bulgaria after four projectile strikes; all 19 crew survive
summary: The Liberian-flagged Gas Husky was hit four times before sinking off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast with 3,400 tonnes of LPG aboard; all 19 Filipino crew were rescued, in the second merchant-ship loss in Bulgarian waters in 24 hours.
content:
A liquefied petroleum gas tanker sank off Bulgaria's Black Sea coast on Tuesday after being struck by four projectiles, in the latest attack on commercial shipping in a stretch of water that has become one of the most dangerous for merchant vessels anywhere in the world. All 19 crew members survived.

The Liberian-flagged Gas Husky was carrying 3,400 metric tons of LPG from Alexandria in Egypt to Midia in Romania when it sent a distress signal on Tuesday morning and began to sink about 50 miles (80 km) east of the town of Byala, according to [Reuters](https://www.gmanetwork.com/news/pinoyabroad/dispatch/1009988/lpg-tanker-with-filipinos-onboard-that-sank-off-bulgaria-was-hit-by-projectiles-official-says/story/), citing a regional governor and maritime security sources.

The all-Filipino crew abandoned the vessel and were found in a life raft before being flown by military helicopter to the Chaika naval air base. The Philippine secretary for migrant workers, Hans Leo Cacdac, confirmed that all 19 were safe and sound, with two of them treated for minor injuries. The men were later taken to a hotel while arrangements were made for their return home.

Mario Smarkov, the regional governor of Varna, said there was no doubt about the number of strikes. "There is no doubt about the number of strikes, there were four, but we have no confirmation from the sailors about the kind of drones used," he said. Two maritime security sources told Reuters the tanker had been hit by an unmanned system, and the captain said the ship was struck four times, including hits on the bridge and the engine room. No party has been blamed for the attack.

Bulgarian officials were initially cautious about the cause. The Defence Ministry said on Tuesday that there was no conclusive evidence and that an investigation was under way, while aerial reconnaissance located an overturned hull in the search area. The Gas Husky, built in 2012 and managed by Stealth Maritime Corporation of Athens, was owned by Octopus Gas Inc. The Greece-based manager did not respond to a request for comment on Wednesday.

The sinking was the second loss of a merchant vessel in Bulgarian waters within 24 hours, after another ship capsized on Monday and its 12 crew members were also rescued, bringing the total saved across both incidents to 31. The tanker joins a growing list of ships struck in the Black Sea in recent weeks, a pattern that has raised concern among NATO members and commercial operators using the busy corridor between Europe and the Caucasus.

The scale of that pattern is the part of the story the first reports barely touched. At least 17 vessels have been attacked off the coasts of Bulgaria and Romania since mid-July, according to maritime security firm Diaplous, yet no government or group has publicly been blamed for any of them, and no authority has said what weapon was used in this latest sinking. The attacks are being treated as separate incidents, but the numbers describe a campaign: commercial ships carrying energy cargoes through waters that NATO states patrol, being hit again and again while the question of who is behind it goes unanswered.

A second gap is what happens to the ship and its cargo now. Officials have said nothing about the 3,400 metric tons of LPG the Gas Husky was carrying — whether it went down with the vessel, whether any of it leaked, or whether the wreck poses a pollution or explosion risk. An overturned hull has been located, but there has been no word on salvage, on containing the cargo, or on how long the wreck will sit on the seabed off Byala.

A third gap is what the shipping industry does next. The route the Gas Husky was sailing, from Egypt to Romania, is an ordinary commercial run, and the crews working it are mostly Filipino seafarers far from home. Each new attack pushes up war-risk insurance and forces owners to weigh whether the Black Sea is still worth the risk. Tankers have become targets elsewhere too, as [Global Wire reported](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/us-destroys-five-iranian-tankers-iran-retaliates-jordan-november-2026) when the United States destroyed five Iranian oil tankers this month, but the Black Sea attacks are different: nobody claims them, nobody explains them, and the ships keep sailing.

The timing adds a further layer. The sinking came in the same week that the leaders of the United States, China and Russia met in Shenzhen to discuss Ukraine and global security, as [Global Wire reported](https://new-sfeed.lovable.app/en/articles/xi-trump-putin-summit-shenzhen-november-19), and while fighting in Ukraine continues to spill into the Black Sea. The Gas Husky was not a warship and carried no military cargo, yet it was hit four times in open water — a reminder that the war's reach now extends to any vessel that happens to be in the wrong stretch of sea.

What happens next depends on Bulgaria's investigation, which is still under way. The crew will be flown home, the wreck will have to be dealt with, and shipowners and insurers will be watching for the findings — and for whether the next vessel through these waters is attacked too. Until someone is named and the weapon is identified, the 17-attack tally will keep growing as a statistic without an explanation, and the seafarers who work the Black Sea will keep sailing a route where a distress signal can come at any moment.
